concepts.name: Sources of history: types, strengths, weaknesses and contributions
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). Written sources, archaeology, oral tradition (oral history) and visual and other sources; the advantages and disadvantages of each; how historians combine them; the contribution of each to recovering pre-colonial history in Zimbabwe and southern Africa (for example archaeology at Great Zimbabwe and Mapungubwe, rock art, oral traditions of states, Portuguese and Arab documents, linguistic evidence). OUT: judging one particular source in an exam question (skills.source-evaluation).

concepts.name: Analysing and evaluating historical sources
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Forms 5-6; Cambridge AS Level). Message, inference and tone; provenance (author, date, audience, purpose); reliability and usefulness; bias and point of view against value judgements; comparing two sources for similarities and differences and explaining them from context (Cambridge Paper 1 part (a), 15 marks); building an argument about how far a set of sources supports a statement, using all the sources and own knowledge (Paper 1 part (b), 25 marks); evidence for ZIMSEC's 'interpret historical evidence' objective. Taught on a range of invented sources from different periods; no new period knowledge. OUT: types of source (skills.sources-of-history); historians' interpretations (skills.interpretations-and-approach).

concepts.name: Writing historical arguments: explanation and judgement
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Forms 5-6; Cambridge AS Level). The command words both boards use (describe, explain, to what extent, how far, assess, evaluate, how successful); the historical concepts of cause and consequence, change and continuity and significance; planning, a clear line of argument, selecting precise evidence, criteria for judging, balanced consideration of other factors, linking back to the question and a supported conclusion. Applies to ZIMSEC Papers 1 and 2 (four 25-mark essays in three hours) and Cambridge Paper 2 (part (a) 10 marks, part (b) 20 marks) and Paper 4 (30 marks). Worked on examples from several periods. OUT: source and extract questions.

concepts.name: Historians' interpretations and approaches: reading an extract
concepts.description: Cambridge only (A Level only). What an interpretation and an approach are and how they are related; why historians differ (fragmentary evidence, selection and interpretation of evidence, new evidence and the passing of time, the time and place in which a historian writes, ideology and beliefs, the questions asked); reading an unattributed extract of up to 600 words for its main claim, its argument and its approach; using own knowledge to explain and test the interpretation; treating the extract as a whole (Cambridge Paper 3, 40 marks, 50% knowledge and 50% interpretations). Taught with invented extracts on topics outside the three prescribed Paper 3 topics. OUT: the content of the three debates (ww1-debate, holocaust and coldwar concepts).

concepts.name: San and Khoi-Khoi societies and their indigenous knowledge systems
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). Internal organisation of the San (hunter-gatherer bands, kinship, leadership, division of labour, beliefs and rock art) and Khoi-Khoi (pastoral herders, clans and chiefs, cattle, trade) societies; their indigenous knowledge systems (medicine, paint, poison, hunting methods and knowledge of the environment) and the impact of these on present societies; relations with Bantu-speaking farmers. OUT: the Bantu migrations themselves (precolonial.bantu-migrations); the detail of the Stone Age tool sequence.

concepts.name: The Bantu migrations: origins, theories, causes and impact
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). Where Bantu-speaking peoples came from (the west-central African origin supported by linguistic and archaeological evidence); the main theories of the migrations (and that they are debated); causes (population growth, search for land, iron-working and farming, environmental change, conflict); routes into eastern and southern Africa and the dating in outline; the impact on the societies already there (San and Khoi-Khoi) and on the development of Iron Age farming communities and states in southern Africa. Contested points are presented as such.

concepts.name: How pre-colonial states arose and were organised: theories and common features
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). The frame used for the state concepts that follow: theories on the origins of pre-colonial states in sub-Saharan Africa (trade, surplus from farming and cattle, iron technology, religion and ritual leadership, conquest and migration, environment); the common political, economic, social and religious features of internal organisation; how organisation helped states develop and expand. Uses a few contrasting examples briefly. OUT: the history of any single state (each has its own concept).

concepts.name: Mapungubwe and Great Zimbabwe
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). Mapungubwe (Limpopo-Shashe region) and Great Zimbabwe: location, origins and the controversies about who built them (the myths of foreign builders and how archaeology showed an African origin), construction, political, economic, social and religious organisation, trade in gold, ivory and cattle and links with the Indian Ocean trade, and the factors argued to explain decline (which historians still debate). OUT: the later states of the plateau (precolonial.mutapa, precolonial.torwa-rozvi).

concepts.name: The Mutapa state
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). Origins in the fifteenth century (Mutota and Matope), expansion, political, economic, social and religious organisation (the mambo, tribute, trade in gold and ivory, the role of spirit mediums), relations with the Portuguese and the reasons for decline (civil war, Portuguese interference, the rise of the Rozvi, succession disputes). Portuguese activities as such are contact.portuguese.

concepts.name: The Torwa and Rozvi states
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). The Torwa state and Khami, the origins of the Rozvi under Changamire Dombo (late seventeenth century), the expulsion of the Portuguese from the plateau, organisation (the Mambo, tribute, cattle, trade, stone building at sites such as Khami, Danangombe and Naletale), religious role of Mwari, and the decline of the Rozvi (nineteenth-century Nguni invasions and internal weakness).

concepts.name: The Ndebele state in Zimbabwe
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). Mzilikazi's migration from the Zulu kingdom to the Transvaal and across the Limpopo (1830s), the formation of the state in south-western Zimbabwe, political, military, economic and social organisation (the king, izinduna, amabutho, raiding and tribute, incorporation of Nguni, Sotho and Shona), the reign of Lobengula and the internal and external pressures that undermined the state. The 1893-94 war is colonisation.anglo-ndebele-war; the Mfecane background is precolonial.mfecane-zulu.

concepts.name: The Mfecane and the Zulu state
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). The causes of the Mfecane and the debate about its scale and causes (population pressure, drought, trade in ivory and slaves, the rise of Dingiswayo's confederacy; some historians argue the Mfecane has been overstated), the rise of the Zulu state under Shaka, his military reforms, the organisation of the state, expansion and the consequences across southern and central Africa, the successors of Shaka and the factors in the decline of the Zulu state (including the Anglo-Zulu War of 1879). Names and dates are given only where well established.

concepts.name: The Gaza state
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). Soshangane's flight from the Zulu kingdom, the founding of the Gaza state in southern Mozambique and south-eastern Zimbabwe in the 1820s, its political and military organisation, trade and relations with the Portuguese, the reign of Ngungunyana and the conquest of the state by the Portuguese in 1895 (decline: internal rivalry and external pressure).

concepts.name: The Mandinka states of West Africa
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). The Mande heritage (Mali empire) as background; the Mandinka state of Samori Toure in the nineteenth century: origins, army and its weapons, economy and trade, the role of Islam in organisation, resistance to French expansion and the reasons for its fall (capture in 1898). Used as a West African comparison with the Zimbabwean and southern African states. OUT: the Scramble itself (imperialism.berlin-partition).

concepts.name: The decline of pre-colonial states: internal and external factors compared
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). Comparing the factors in the decline of the states studied (Great Zimbabwe, Mutapa, Rozvi, Ndebele, Zulu, Gaza, Mandinka): internal (succession disputes, rebellion of subject peoples, environmental and economic strain) against external (migration and invasion, trade shifts, European intervention); building a reasoned judgement about which mattered more. An essay-skill lesson on knowledge covered in the single-state concepts, with new comparative frameworks and examples.

concepts.name: Contacts with Persia, China, India and Arabia: the Indian Ocean trade
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). The Indian Ocean trade network and the Swahili coast (Sofala and Kilwa), contacts of Zimbabwean societies with Persian, Arab, Indian and Chinese merchants; goods exchanged (gold, ivory, copper, cattle products against cloth, beads and ceramics) and archaeological evidence at Great Zimbabwe and other sites; the nature of the activities and their impact on the societies of the plateau (wealth, state formation, dependence on trade). OUT: the Portuguese (contact.portuguese).

concepts.name: The Portuguese and the Zimbabwean plateau
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). Portuguese arrival on the east coast (from 1498), trading posts (Sofala, Sena and Tete), the prazo system, the activities of the Jesuit missionary Goncalo da Silveira (killed in 1561), military expeditions, the trade in gold and ivory, interference in the Mutapa state and its succession, and the impact on Zimbabwean societies until their expulsion from the plateau in the 1690s. OUT: the Mutapa state as such (precolonial.mutapa).

concepts.name: Missionaries, hunters, traders, explorers and concession seekers
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). The individuals and groups who reached Zimbabwean societies in the nineteenth century: missionaries (the London Missionary Society mission at Inyati from 1859, the Jesuits from 1879), hunters and traders, explorers (for example Karl Mauch's visit to Great Zimbabwe in 1871) and concession seekers; their activities and their impact on the Ndebele and Shona. OUT: the concession that led to occupation (colonisation.occupation).

concepts.name: Britain, Germany, the Transvaal and the Orange Free State in Zimbabwe before 1888
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). Why each state was interested (minerals, land, trade, strategic and imperial rivalry in southern Africa), their agents and diplomacy at the court of Lobengula, treaty-making (the Grobler Treaty of 1887, the Moffat Treaty of 1888) and the impact on Ndebele independence. OUT: the Rudd Concession onwards (colonisation.occupation).

concepts.name: The abolition of the slave trade: reasons, process and impact on Africa
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). Humanitarian, economic and political reasons for abolition; the process (British abolition of the trade in 1807 and of slavery in 1833-34, patrols of the West Africa Squadron, treaties with African rulers, the position in the United States, France, Brazil and in East Africa and Zanzibar); the effects on African societies (economic dislocation, political change, resettlement at Freetown and Liberia, the shift to other trades). OUT: legitimate trade as such (slavery.legitimate-trade).

concepts.name: The transition to legitimate trade
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). Reasons for the transition (industrial demand for palm oil, groundnuts, rubber and ivory; abolition; changing African interests), states and societies that switched successfully and those that failed in West and East Africa (for example the Niger Delta states and the rise of Opobo under Jaja; the position of Dahomey, Asante and Zanzibar), and the impact on African societies: growth of towns and ports, emergence of powerful states such as Opobo, instability, and European interference that led to colonisation.

concepts.name: The causes of the Scramble for Africa
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). Economic, political and strategic, humanitarian and religious motives; the role of technology and medicine (steamships, the Maxim gun, quinine); rivalry among European powers; African conditions that made colonisation possible; and how historians weigh the causes (the explanations are debated). OUT: the conference and the partition itself (imperialism.berlin-partition).

concepts.name: The Berlin Conference and the partition of Africa
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). Why the conference met (Bismarck's chairmanship, rival claims on the Congo and Niger), the terms of the Berlin Conference of 1884-85 (free trade, navigation, effective occupation, notification of claims, the recognition of the Congo Free State's claim), the absence of African representatives, the process of partition by treaty and agreement, and the effects on Africa (borders, loss of sovereignty, exploitation, resistance) and on Europe (rivalry and tension).

concepts.name: The occupation of Zimbabwe to 1890
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). Reasons for the colonisation of Zimbabwe (the mineral expectations, Rhodes's ambitions, rivalry with the Portuguese, the Transvaal and Germany); the steps to 1890: the Moffat Treaty (1888), the Rudd Concession (30 October 1888) and how it was disputed, the Royal Charter (29 October 1889) and the British South Africa Company, the Pioneer Column and the hoisting of the flag at Fort Salisbury (12 September 1890); the role of Chaminuka's warnings in Shona oral tradition (presented as tradition). OUT: the war of 1893-94 (colonisation.anglo-ndebele-war).

concepts.name: The Anglo-Ndebele War of 1893-94
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). Causes (the Company's wish for Matabeleland, the Victoria incident of July 1893, differing views of the Rudd Concession), the events (the advance on Bulawayo, the battles on the Shangani and Bembesi in the Maxim-gun war, the Shangani Patrol, the fall of Bulawayo in November 1893 and Lobengula's flight and death in 1894) and the results for the Ndebele (land and cattle, the Matabeleland Order in Council, loss of independence).

concepts.name: Causes of the 1896-97 Umvukela and Chimurenga
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). Grievances in Matabeleland and Mashonaland: loss of land and cattle, forced labour and the Native Police, taxation, the effects of rinderpest and the slaughter of cattle, drought and locusts, and loss of political independence; the role of religious leaders in organising; the debate over how far the two risings were coordinated. OUT: the course (risings.course-results).

concepts.name: Course and results of the First Chimurenga/Umvukela
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). The outbreak in Matabeleland (March 1896) and in Mashonaland (June 1896), the main events (attacks in Matabeleland, the siege of Bulawayo, Mazowe and the Shona risings), the Matopos indabas with Rhodes (October 1896), the continuation in Mashonaland and the end of fighting in 1897, the capture and execution of Kaguvi and Nehanda (executed in April 1898), and the results (loss of life, increased colonial control, administrative changes, hardship).

concepts.name: Spirit mediums, leaders and the reasons for African defeat in 1896-97
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). The role of spirit mediums and religious leaders (Nehanda, Kaguvi, Mlimo/Mkwati and others), chiefs and military leaders in the Chimurenga and the Umvukela and the part played by women; the reasons for African defeat (weapons, lack of unity and central command, famine and disease, colonial reinforcement and divide-and-rule); and why the risings were remembered as inspiration for later nationalism.

concepts.name: Company rule, 1890-1923
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). The nature of administration by the British South Africa Company (the Charter, the Administrator, the Legislative Council, the Native Department and Native Commissioners), land alienation and reserves, taxes and forced labour, mining and the settler economy, African grievances, and the end of Company rule (the 1922 referendum and the grant of responsible government from 1923). OUT: settler rule after 1923 (colonial.settler-rule-legislation).

concepts.name: Settler rule, 1923-1965: laws, segregation and the Federation
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). Responsible government from 1923; the segregationist legislation (Land Apportionment Act 1930, Industrial Conciliation Act 1934, Native Registration, the Land Husbandry Act of 1951), African reactions, urbanisation and labour, the Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland (1953-1963); the impact on African land, work, education and political rights. OUT: UDI and after (colonial.udi-rhodesian-front).

concepts.name: The Rhodesian Front, UDI and sanctions, 1962-1979
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). The Rhodesian Front's election in 1962, Ian Smith's government, Unilateral Declaration of Independence (11 November 1965), British and United Nations sanctions and how Rhodesia coped, the failed settlement talks (HMS Tiger 1966, HMS Fearless 1968, the Pearce Commission 1972), the Land Tenure Act of 1969, the republic of 1970 and the internal settlement of 1978-79; the impact on Africans and on the economy.

concepts.name: Ethiopia under Menelik II: resistance to Italy
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). Menelik II's rise and modernisation, the Treaty of Wuchale (1889) and the dispute over its Italian and Amharic versions, Italian ambitions, the war and the Battle of Adwa (1 March 1896), the Treaty of Addis Ababa and its results (Ethiopia remained independent; the effect on African and Pan-African opinion); causes, nature and results of the resistance, including diplomacy as well as arms.

concepts.name: The Maji Maji Uprising in German East Africa, 1905-1907
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). Causes (forced cotton growing and labour, taxes, abuses by German officials and their agents), the leadership of Kinjikitile and the maji medicine, the outbreak in July 1905 and spread across many peoples, the course and German suppression (including scorched-earth tactics and famine), the heavy loss of life (estimates are very uncertain and given as a range), and an assessment of the effectiveness of the methods used.

concepts.name: The armed struggle in Mozambique
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). Colonial rule and forced labour under Portugal, the formation of FRELIMO (1962) under Eduardo Mondlane, the start of the armed struggle (1964), its course, the leadership of Samora Machel, Portuguese counter-measures, the contribution of foreign states (Tanzania, Zambia, the OAU, China and the USSR among others), the fall of the Portuguese regime in 1974 and independence in 1975.

concepts.name: Early African nationalism to 1957: from trade unions to mass nationalism
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). Early organisations in Southern Rhodesia (welfare and voters' associations, the ICU branch, trade unions and strikes such as 1945 and 1948, the City Youth League of 1955) and the formation of the Southern Rhodesia African National Congress in 1957; why unionism gave way to mass nationalism and the effects of the Federation of 1953.

concepts.name: The nationalist parties: NDP, ZAPU and ZANU
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). The National Democratic Party (1960), ZAPU (1961), the split of 1963 and the formation of ZANU, leaders, support and policies, banning and detention, and how repression and the split shaped the turn to armed struggle. OUT: military events (liberation.armed-struggle-1966-72 and 1972-79).

concepts.name: Causes of the Second Chimurenga and attempts to end the war peacefully
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). Causes (land alienation, discrimination, loss of political rights, repression, UDI, failure of constitutional methods, the decolonisation of Africa); and the peaceful attempts: the failed talks on HMS Tiger and HMS Fearless, the Pearce Commission, the Victoria Falls Conference of 1975, Geneva 1976, the Anglo-American proposals and the internal settlement of 1978. OUT: Lancaster House (liberation.lancaster-house).

concepts.name: The armed struggle, 1966-1972
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). Early sabotage, the Battle of Chinhoyi (28 April 1966), the Wankie and Sipolilo campaigns of 1967-68, training abroad (including China and the USSR), the roles of ZANLA and ZIPRA, Rhodesian counter-measures, and the reasons why the first phase did not succeed.

concepts.name: The armed struggle, 1972-1979
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). The Altena Farm attack of 21 December 1972 and the new phase from the north-east using Mozambique, mobilisation of the rural population (pungwe), the Rhodesian response (protected villages, Selous Scouts, cross-border raids such as Nyadzonia in 1976 and Chimoio in 1977), the Patriotic Front, the growing pressure of the war on Rhodesia; casualty figures only as widely accepted estimates.

concepts.name: Roles in the liberation struggle and its impact on Africans
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). The roles of spirit mediums, peasants, women, chiefs, churches, nationalist organisations and war collaborators; the effects of the war on African communities (displacement, protected villages, loss of life, disruption of schools and health services, the refugee flows); balanced treatment of different groups' experiences.

concepts.name: The Lancaster House Conference and the 1980 settlement
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). Why the conference was convened (the war, sanctions, the failure of the internal settlement, the Commonwealth meeting at Lusaka in 1979, the pressure of the Frontline States), the delegations, the main provisions (the independence constitution with seats reserved for whites, protection of property and land arrangements, the ceasefire and transition under a British governor), the elections of February 1980 and independence on 18 April 1980; advantages and disadvantages of the settlement.

concepts.name: Political developments, 1980-2000: reconciliation and the Unity Accord
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). The 1980 government of national unity (its composition), the policy of reconciliation and its impact, the political challenges (integration of armies, dissidents, the disturbances in Matabeleland and the Midlands in the 1980s acknowledged factually, the dismissal of Nkomo in 1982), the Unity Accord of 22 December 1987 and its terms, and later political developments to 2000.

concepts.name: Economic developments, 1980-2000: blueprints, achievements and challenges
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). Government economic blueprints (Growth with Equity 1981, the Transitional National Development Plan, the first Five-Year National Development Plan, ESAP from 1991 and ZIMPREST), achievements (for example in smallholder agriculture and social spending in the 1980s) and challenges (droughts, balance of payments deficits, debt, external interference, the effects of ESAP, 1997); no unsourced statistics.

concepts.name: Social developments, 1980-2000: education, health and human rights
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). Expansion of education (free primary schooling, secondary and tertiary growth), health (primary health care, immunisation, clinics), other social developments (housing, women's legal status) compared with the period before independence, and social challenges (HIV/AIDS, user fees and cuts under ESAP, unemployment); human-rights developments in outline.

concepts.name: Zimbabwe's foreign policy, 1980-2000
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). ZIMSEC detail (scope and sequence only): non-alignment and the Non-Aligned Movement, the Frontline States and SADCC, opposition to apartheid and support to Mozambique, relations with the Commonwealth, the UN and the OAU, and the intervention in the Democratic Republic of Congo in 1998 as part of SADC; presented neutrally with aims and different views.

concepts.name: Indigenisation, empowerment and enterprise skills
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). Indigenisation and empowerment policies after independence (affirmative action, indigenisation of the civil service, the security sector and local councils, support for black business, later legislation), their implementation, business models that promote indigenisation and national pride (cooperatives, community share ownership, SMEs), successes, challenges and different views.

concepts.name: Land reform 1980-1999: theory and practice
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). The land question inherited at independence, the laws governing land reform (the Lancaster House terms, the Land Acquisition Acts of 1985 and 1992, the constitutional amendments), resettlement models, the implementation of the policy and its successes and difficulties, criticisms from different sides, and the 1998 donors' conference.

concepts.name: Land reform after 2000: the Third Chimurenga
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). Reasons for the fast-track land reform (slow resettlement, the Lancaster House constraints, the referendum of February 2000, pressure from war veterans and landless people), the laws after 2000, the course of the programme, its impact (agricultural production, land tenure, the economy, relations with Britain and the sanctions debate); different views fairly presented; no slogans.

concepts.name: Protection of intellectual property
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). ZIMSEC detail: what intellectual property is (patents, copyright, trade marks, industrial designs, and traditional knowledge), the laws and regulations in Zimbabwe, the institutions (the Zimbabwe Intellectual Property Office and regional and international bodies such as ARIPO and WIPO), government efforts to enforce registration, successes and challenges for individuals and institutions.

concepts.name: Human rights and responsibilities
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). Human rights and the duties that accompany them, the Declaration of Rights in the 2013 Constitution and international instruments such as the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the rights of children, the efforts of the government and institutions (including the Zimbabwe Human Rights Commission) in promoting rights, and criticisms and different views.

concepts.name: Democracy in Zimbabwe: types, organs of government and efforts
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). Characteristics and types of democracy (direct, representative, liberal, and other forms), the roles of the executive, the legislature and the judiciary and the separation of powers under the Constitution of Zimbabwe, elections and citizen participation, devolution, and the government's efforts to promote democracy, with strengths, weaknesses and different views.

concepts.name: The Ancien Regime, the crisis of 1787-89 and the outbreak of revolution
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Forms 5-6; Cambridge AS Level). Absolute monarchy and royal government; the Estates and the discontent of the Third Estate; the influence of the Enlightenment and the American War of Independence; the financial problems and attempted reforms (Turgot, Necker, Calonne); the Assembly of Notables; the crisis of 1787-89 and bad harvests; the Estates-General, the cahiers and the National Assembly; the Tennis Court Oath; the storming of the Bastille, the Great Fear, the August Decrees, the Declaration of the Rights of Man and the March of the Women (Cambridge key question 1.1; ZIMSEC causes of the Revolution).

concepts.name: From constitutional monarchy to republic, 1789-1792
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Forms 5-6; Cambridge AS Level). Revolutionary groups (Jacobins, Feuillants, Girondins) and counter-revolutionary groups; the reforms (assignats, taxation, local government, justice, the Church); political instability (the constitution, the flight to Varennes, the Champ de Mars); the Legislative Assembly, the war with Austria (April 1792), the September Massacres and the abolition of the monarchy by the National Convention (Cambridge key question 1.2; ZIMSEC events of the Revolution).

concepts.name: The Republic at war: Terror, Thermidor and the Directory, 1793-1799
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Forms 5-6; Cambridge AS Level). Problems after Louis XVI's execution, the sans-culottes and divisions in the Convention, the effects of war, the Constitution of 1793, the Committee of Public Safety, Robespierre and the Terror, economic controls, the Thermidorian reaction and the White Terror, the Parisian risings of 1795, the Constitution of the Year III and the Directory with its successes and failures (Cambridge key question 1.3; ZIMSEC events).

concepts.name: Napoleon Bonaparte: rise, authoritarian control and domestic reforms
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Forms 5-6; Cambridge AS Level). Napoleon's military reputation and ambitions, the coup of 1799, the consulate and the Empire (1804), the means of authoritarian control (ministries, the Council of State, police, censorship and propaganda, plebiscites), and the domestic reforms (the Napoleonic Code, education, the Bank of France and the economy, the Concordat) (Cambridge key question 1.4, first part; ZIMSEC rise of Napoleon and domestic policies).

concepts.name: Napoleon's wars and empire, and the reasons for his fall
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Forms 5-6; Cambridge AS Level). ZIMSEC: Napoleon's foreign policy and the impact of his policies on France and Europe. Cambridge: only the reasons for his fall (declining popularity at home, the failure of the Continental System, the Peninsular War, the growth of nationalism, the Russian campaign of 1812, Leipzig in 1813, the capture of Paris and abdication in 1814); military campaigns are covered in outline, not in detail.

concepts.name: The impact of the French Revolution on France and the world
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). ZIMSEC detail: the changes in France (legal equality, the end of feudal privileges, secularisation, the new administration), the spread of revolutionary ideas of liberty and equality, the influence on Europe, on nationalism and on movements elsewhere (for example Haiti and the Americas), and the immediate response of other powers; assessing what changed and what did not.

concepts.name: The Vienna Settlement and the Congress System
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). ZIMSEC detail: the aims and principles of the Congress of Vienna (legitimacy, balance of power, compensation and containing France), the leading statesmen, the territorial settlement, an assessment of the settlement, the Congress System (Aix-la-Chapelle, Troppau, Laibach and Verona) and the reasons for its collapse.

concepts.name: The Restored Bourbons in France, 1814-1830
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). ZIMSEC detail: the reign of Louis XVIII (the Charter of 1814, the ultra-royalists, the White Terror of 1815) and Charles X (Villele, Polignac, the July Ordinances of 1830) and the reasons for the Bourbons' fall in the July Revolution of 1830.

concepts.name: The unification of Italy
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). ZIMSEC detail: the background (Napoleonic reorganisation, the Vienna settlement, secret societies, Mazzini and Young Italy, the revolutions of 1820, 1831 and 1848-49), the role of Piedmont-Sardinia, Cavour (Plombieres and the war of 1859), Garibaldi and the Thousand, the proclamation of the Kingdom of Italy in 1861 and the completion with Venetia (1866) and Rome (1870); the role of foreign powers and an assessment of who contributed most.

concepts.name: Germany from 1815 to the eve of the 1848 revolutions
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Forms 5-6; Cambridge AS Level). The Congress of Vienna and the German Confederation (strengths and weaknesses), Metternich's system and the Carlsbad Decrees, liberal ideas and the emerging middle class, the growth of nationalism (the 1830 revolutions, the universities, the Six and Ten Articles of 1832), the Zollverein and railways, and the economic and social problems of the 1840s including the crisis of 1846-47 (Cambridge key question 2.1; ZIMSEC background to unification).

concepts.name: The revolutions of 1848-49 in the German states
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Forms 5-6; Cambridge AS Level). The spread of revolution and the fall of Metternich, revolution in Prussia and the role of Friedrich Wilhelm IV, the Frankfurt Parliament and the reasons for its collapse, the reasons why the conservatives reasserted control, and the impact of the revolutions (Cambridge key question 2.2, first part).

concepts.name: Austria and Prussia, 1849-1862
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Forms 5-6; Cambridge AS Level). Changing relations between Austria and Prussia after 1848 (the humiliation of Olmutz), economic issues (the Zollverein dispute, Prussian economic growth against Austria's financial problems), political issues (the growth of liberalism, Prussia's international position) and Bismarck's role up to 1859 and his attitude to Austria (Cambridge key question 2.2, second part).

concepts.name: Bismarck's rise and the defeat of Austria, 1862-1866
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Forms 5-6; Cambridge AS Level). The constitutional crisis, Wilhelm I and army reform, Bismarck's appointment and how he resolved the crisis; the Congress of Princes of 1863; the war with Denmark (1864) and its outcome; the preparation for war with Austria (Biarritz, the alliance with Italy); the Seven Weeks' War, the Treaty of Prague, the North German Confederation and the Indemnity Bill (Cambridge key question 2.3).

concepts.name: The completion of German unification, 1866-1871
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Forms 5-6; Cambridge AS Level). Pressure from nationalists, the problem of the southern states (the Zollparlament), Napoleon III's ambitions and the Luxemburg crisis, the Hohenzollern candidature and the Ems Telegram, the Franco-Prussian War (Sedan, the armistice of January 1871, the Treaty of Frankfurt) and the creation and constitution of the German Empire in 1871 (Cambridge key question 2.4; ZIMSEC unification of Germany).

concepts.name: Long-term causes of the First World War, c.1890-1914
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Forms 5-6; Cambridge A Level only). Tensions between the Great Powers, the alliance system and the diplomatic revolution, militarism and the arms and naval races, imperial and economic rivalry (the Moroccan crises), instability in the Balkans, the war plans (including the Schlieffen Plan) and nationalism; the relative weight of long-term factors. Shared by ZIMSEC (causes of the war) and Cambridge Paper 3 Topic 1 (the context for the debate). OUT: the crisis of June-August 1914 (ww1.july-crisis).

concepts.name: The July Crisis of 1914 and the outbreak of war
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Forms 5-6; Cambridge A Level only). The assassination at Sarajevo (28 June 1914), the German 'blank cheque', the Austrian ultimatum and Serbia's reply, mobilisations and declarations of war, the invasion of Belgium and Britain's entry; the decisions of key individuals and the role of chance and contingency in the outbreak. Shared by ZIMSEC and Cambridge Paper 3.

concepts.name: The course of the First World War
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). ZIMSEC detail: the main events on the Western and Eastern fronts, at sea and in the colonies including Africa, new weapons and trench warfare, the entry of the United States (1917), Russia's withdrawal and the end of the war in 1918; kept to events and turning points, not strategy debates.

concepts.name: The results and impact of the First World War
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). ZIMSEC detail: human losses (labelled estimates), political results (the fall of four empires), economic and social effects including the role of women and the influenza pandemic, territorial changes, and the impact on Africa (former German colonies as mandates, African soldiers and carriers) and on the world.

concepts.name: The Paris Peace Settlement
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). ZIMSEC detail: the Paris Peace Conference of 1919, the aims of the leading statesmen (Wilson and his Fourteen Points, Clemenceau, Lloyd George), the Treaty of Versailles and the other treaties, German reactions, the mandate system, and an assessment of whether the settlement was fair or workable.

concepts.name: The League of Nations: aims, work and collapse
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). ZIMSEC detail: the origins and aims of the League, its organisation, its successes and failures in the 1920s and 1930s (disputes, humanitarian agencies, Manchuria and Abyssinia), and the factors that led to its collapse.

concepts.name: Who was to blame for the First World War? Responsibility from Article 231 to the Fischer thesis
concepts.description: Cambridge only (A Level only). Paper 3 Topic 1 (A Level only): Article 231 and its effect on the debate, the idea of shared responsibility in the 1920s and 1930s, the effect of the Second World War, Fritz Fischer's thesis of the 1960s, the German reaction and the challenges to Fischer. Historians' positions are paraphrased; no invented quotations. OUT: the events themselves (ww1.long-term-causes, ww1.july-crisis).

concepts.name: Modern interpretations of the origins of the First World War
concepts.description: Cambridge only (A Level only). Paper 3 Topic 1 (A Level only): interpretations that explore the responsibility of countries other than Germany, the relative weight of long-term and short-term factors, the importance of key individuals' decisions, contingency over motive, and how the centenary of 1914 affected the debate; works named only where certain (for example Christopher Clark's The Sleepwalkers, 2012).

concepts.name: Mussolini: the rise of Fascism and the establishment of a dictatorship, 1919-1926
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Forms 5-6; Cambridge A Level only). Italy's problems after the First World War (the 'mutilated victory', Fiume, unemployment and inflation, the Biennio Rosso, unstable governments); the Fascist movement and squadrismo; the March on Rome and Mussolini's appointment in 1922; the role of Victor Emmanuel III and the elites; the establishment of a dictatorship 1922-26 (the Acerbo Law, the Matteotti murder, the laws of 1925-26) (Cambridge key question 1.1; ZIMSEC rise of Mussolini 1919-22).

concepts.name: How effectively did Mussolini govern Italy? Terror, propaganda, institutions and foreign policy
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Forms 5-6; Cambridge A Level only). The terror state (OVRA, special tribunals, the antisemitic laws of 1938), propaganda and censorship (the personality cult, the Ministry of Popular Culture, media, rallies, art and sport), the nature of Fascist government (Duce, Fascist Party, Grand Council, prefects and podestas) and foreign policy (aims, Corfu, Albania, the invasion of Abyssinia, alliances with Germany) (Cambridge key question 1.2).

concepts.name: Mussolini's economic policies
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Forms 5-6; Cambridge A Level only). Attempts to modernise the economy (the 'battles' for the lira, grain and land, autarky), the response to the Great Depression (IMI and IRI, public works), the Corporate State, and living standards (welfare, pay, working hours, consumption) (Cambridge key question 1.3).

concepts.name: How far did Mussolini transform Italian society?
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Forms 5-6; Cambridge A Level only). Fascist policies towards women and the family (the Battle for Births), young people and education (the Gentile reforms, the Opera Nazionale Balilla), religion (the Lateran Treaties and later tensions), mass organisations (OND), and the extent of opposition (Cambridge key question 1.4).

concepts.name: Hitler: the rise of the Nazis and the creation of a dictatorship, 1929-1934
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Forms 5-6; Cambridge A Level only). ZIMSEC detail: the background 1919-29 (the early party, the Munich Putsch, Mein Kampf). Both boards: the effects of the Great Depression on Weimar governments, the growth of Nazi support 1929-32 (Hitler's appeal, the SA, propaganda, elite support), the elections of 1932, Hitler's appointment as Chancellor in January 1933, the Reichstag Fire, the Enabling Act, the Night of the Long Knives and the death of Hindenburg (Cambridge key question 3.1).

concepts.name: How effectively did the Nazis govern Germany? Terror, propaganda, opposition and foreign policy
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Forms 5-6; Cambridge A Level only). The terror state (Gestapo, SS, courts, concentration camps), propaganda (Goebbels, media, Nuremberg rallies, the 1936 Olympics), the extent of opposition (youth, churches, the left, passive resistance), and Nazi foreign policy (aims, methods and sequence from leaving the League of Nations to the invasion of Poland and Barbarossa) (Cambridge key question 3.2).

concepts.name: Nazi economic policies
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Forms 5-6; Cambridge A Level only). Responses to the Great Depression (Schacht, deficit financing and public works, the Reich Labour Service), agricultural policies, rearmament and autarky (the New Plan and the Four Year Plan, guns or butter) and living standards (employment, wages, the DAF, Strength through Joy) (Cambridge key question 3.3).

concepts.name: How far did the Nazis transform German society?
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Forms 5-6; Cambridge A Level only). Nazi policies towards women, young people and education (the Hitler Youth), religion (the Concordat, the Reich Church) and the persecution of Jews and other minorities (race theories, the boycott, the Nuremberg Laws, Kristallnacht; other victims) (Cambridge key question 3.4). The Holocaust as a Paper 3 topic is holocaust.nazi-policy-1933-45.

concepts.name: Mussolini and Hitler compared: domestic and foreign policies and their impact on the world
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). ZIMSEC detail: comparing the ideologies, domestic policies and foreign policies of Mussolini and Hitler (similarities and differences), the Axis (Rome-Berlin Axis, Anti-Comintern Pact, Pact of Steel), and the impact of their policies on the world; an essay-skill lesson drawing together the mussolini.* and nazi.* concepts.

concepts.name: Causes of the Second World War
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). ZIMSEC detail: long-term causes (the Treaty of Versailles, the Depression, the dictators, the failure of the League and of collective security, appeasement) and the short-term sequence of 1938-39 (Anschluss, Munich, the occupation of Prague, the Nazi-Soviet Pact, the attack on Poland), with Japan's aggression in Asia.

concepts.name: The course of the Second World War
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). ZIMSEC detail: the main events in Europe, North Africa and the Pacific (the fall of France, Barbarossa, Pearl Harbor, Stalingrad, D-Day, the defeat of Germany, Midway and the atomic bombs), the role of Africa and African soldiers, and the end of the war in 1945; turning points rather than campaign detail.

concepts.name: Results and impact of the Second World War
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). ZIMSEC detail: human losses (labelled estimates), the Nuremberg trials, the division of Germany, the founding of the United Nations, the beginning of the Cold War, economic recovery in Europe, and the effect on colonial empires and African nationalism.

concepts.name: Russia under Alexander III, 1881-1894: the challenges facing the Tsarist regime
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Forms 5-6; Cambridge AS Level). How Russia was ruled (autocracy, the State Council, ministries, the army and Church), reform and repression (Alexander III's policies, Russification), economic development (Bunge's policies, industrialisation, taxation and famine), social change, and the role of opposition including the growth of Marxism (Cambridge key question 3.1; ZIMSEC causes of the Russian Revolution).

concepts.name: The 1905 Revolution and the survival of Tsarism to 1914
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Forms 5-6; Cambridge AS Level). Causes of the 1905 Revolution (discontent under Nicholas II, opposition parties, economic problems, defeat in the Russo-Japanese War), Bloody Sunday, strikes and unrest, the October Manifesto and the Duma, the reasons why the regime survived, and the extent of change to 1914 (Stolypin's reforms, industrial growth) (Cambridge key question 3.2; ZIMSEC 1905).

concepts.name: The February and October Revolutions of 1917
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Forms 5-6; Cambridge AS Level). The impact of the First World War on Tsarist rule, the causes and effects of the February Revolution and the Tsar's abdication, the Provisional Government and the reasons for its failure (the war, land, the July Days, the Kornilov revolt), and how and why the Bolsheviks seized power in October (Lenin, the Petrograd Soviet, Trotsky, the Military Revolutionary Committee). Dates given in the Western calendar with the Russian calendar noted (Cambridge key question 3.3).

concepts.name: Bolshevik consolidation of power, 1917-1924
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Forms 5-6; Cambridge AS Level). Bolshevik policies and decrees, Sovnarkom, the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, the dictatorship (the Cheka, the Constituent Assembly), the Civil War and the reasons for the Bolshevik victory (War Communism; the weaknesses of the Whites), the Kronstadt Mutiny and the New Economic Policy (Cambridge key question 3.4).

concepts.name: Stalin's rise to power, 1924-1929
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Forms 5-6; Cambridge A Level only). The power vacuum after Lenin's death (collective leadership, Lenin's Testament), the strengths and weaknesses of the candidates (Stalin, Trotsky, Bukharin, Zinoviev, Kamenev), the ideological arguments (NEP against rapid industrialisation, Socialism in One Country against Permanent Revolution), changing alliances and the use of party posts, repression and propaganda to 1929 (Cambridge key question 2.1).

concepts.name: How effectively did Stalin govern the Soviet Union? Terror, cult and foreign policy
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Forms 5-6; Cambridge A Level only). Terror and the Purges (Kirov, the NKVD, the show trials, the Yezhovshchina, the gulags and the armed forces), the cult of personality, Stalin's leadership and the 1936 Constitution, and foreign policy (relations with Germany, collective security, the Spanish Civil War, policies towards China and Japan, the Nazi-Soviet Pact) (Cambridge key question 2.2).

concepts.name: Stalin's economic policies: collectivisation and the Five Year Plans
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Forms 5-6; Cambridge A Level only). The reasons for the 'Great Turn', agricultural policies (collectivisation, dekulakisation, the famine and yields), industrial policies (Gosplan, the first three Five Year Plans, the Stakhanovite movement) and living standards of managers and workers (Cambridge key question 2.3). Casualty and production figures given as labelled estimates.

concepts.name: How far did Stalin transform Soviet society?
concepts.description: Both boards (ZIMSEC Forms 5-6; Cambridge A Level only). Women and the family (the 'Great Retreat'), young people and education, cultural change (the Cultural Revolution and Socialist Realism), religious policy and the treatment of national groups (Cambridge key question 2.4).

concepts.name: The Soviet Union in the Second World War, 1941-1945
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). ZIMSEC detail (Russia 1905-1945): the German invasion, Stalingrad and the turn of the war, the role of the Soviet Union in the Allied victory, the costs (labelled estimates), and the effect on Stalin's regime and on Soviet society to 1945.

concepts.name: China's revolutions, 1900-1949
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). ZIMSEC detail: the decline of the Qing, the Boxer Rising, the 1911 Revolution and the Republic, warlords, the May Fourth Movement, the Guomindang and the Chinese Communist Party, the Long March, the war with Japan, the civil war and the People's Republic of 1949 (causes, events and the role of peasant support).

concepts.name: China under Mao Zedong, 1949-1976
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). ZIMSEC detail: land reform and the consolidation of Communist rule, the First Five-Year Plan, the Great Leap Forward and its famine (death estimates vary very widely and are given as a range), the Sino-Soviet split, the Cultural Revolution, and the situation at Mao's death in 1976; an assessment of revolutionary policies.

concepts.name: The Russian and Chinese revolutions compared
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). ZIMSEC detail: causes, leadership, the role of peasants and workers, the party, revolutionary policies on land, industry and control, and similarities and differences between Russia (1905-1945) and China (1900-1976); an essay-skill lesson drawing together the russia.*, stalin.* and china.* concepts.

concepts.name: The United Nations: origins, aims, structure and work
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). Origins in 1945 after the failure of the League, aims and principles of the Charter, the organs (General Assembly, Security Council and the veto, International Court of Justice, Economic and Social Council, Secretariat), specialised agencies, peacekeeping and the UN's work in Africa and Zimbabwe, and the criticisms of the organisation.

concepts.name: From the OAU to the African Union
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). Origins of the OAU (1963) and its aims, its Liberation Committee and role in decolonisation, its weaknesses, the transition to the African Union (2002), the AU's organs and aims, the concept of regional integration and Agenda 2063, achievements and challenges.

concepts.name: SADCC and SADC: regional co-operation and integration
concepts.description: ZIMSEC only (Forms 5-6). The origins of SADCC (1980) and SADC (1992), the aims, the structure (Summit, Council, Secretariat), the concept of integration (free trade area, customs union, common market) and SADC's progress and problems; Zimbabwe's role; successes and challenges.

concepts.name: The Holocaust: antisemitism, persecution and extermination, 1933-1945
concepts.description: Cambridge only (A Level only). Paper 3 Topic 2 context (A Level only): the background of European and German antisemitism and racist theories, Nazi persecution of the Jews 1933-41, the impact of war on Nazi policy (ghettoisation, the Einsatzgruppen, the Wannsee Conference, the extermination camps), Jewish responses, other victims, and contemporary reactions. Told accurately and respectfully, without graphic description; the number of Jewish victims is given as the scholarly estimate of about six million.

concepts.name: The Holocaust debate: intentionalism, structuralism, functionalism and synthesis
concepts.description: Cambridge only (A Level only). Paper 3 Topic 2 (A Level only): whether the Holocaust grew from ideas that pre-dated the Nazis; the role of Hitler and the intentionalist view; the structuralist and functionalist views (the nature of the Nazi state, war and contingent factors); synthesis interpretations that combine them. Historians' positions are paraphrased, with works named only where certain.

concepts.name: The Holocaust debate: perpetrators, victims and bystanders
concepts.description: Cambridge only (A Level only). Paper 3 Topic 2 (A Level only): who carried out the Holocaust and why (the extent of participation, non-German collaborators), how far Jews resisted and how resistance is defined, whether definitions should include other victims, and how the United States and Britain responded at the time.

concepts.name: The origins of the Cold War in Europe, 1941-1949
concepts.description: Cambridge only (A Level only). Paper 3 Topic 3 context (A Level only): tensions in the wartime alliance, problems of peace-making, the Yalta and Potsdam conferences, tensions in a divided Europe, the Truman Doctrine and the Marshall Plan, the Berlin Blockade and Airlift and the formation of NATO.

concepts.name: Who was to blame for the Cold War? Traditionalism, revisionism and post-revisionism
concepts.description: Cambridge only (A Level only). Paper 3 Topic 3 (A Level only): how far tensions were inherent in 1945, the importance of the leaders' personalities, ideology, security and economics, and the three schools (traditionalist interpretations blaming the Soviet Union, revisionist blaming the USA, and post-revisionist blaming both or neither); historians paraphrased and named only where certain.

concepts.name: The Cold War debate: Russian perspectives, new archives and the 'New' Cold War history
concepts.description: Cambridge only (A Level only). Paper 3 Topic 3 (A Level only): how Russian historians' perspectives differ from Western ones, reinterpretations in the light of new archival sources, and the emergence of the 'New' Cold War history (post-post-revisionism).
